Neonates of the silky anteater (Cyclopes didactylus) are remarkably small, weighing only 10 grams [Wwb = 10 grams] at birth, a value that underscores the altricial state of the newborn. This initial mass is minuscule compared to the ultimate body size attained by adult females, which reach an average maximum wet weight of 266 grams [Wwi = 266 grams], though field records indicate considerable variation, with adult females ranging from 175 to 400 grams. The journey from this diminutive start to independence involves a prolonged period of maternal care. The weaning process, marking nutritional independence, occurs at approximately 160 grams [Wwx = approximately 160 grams], a mass that represents a sixteen-fold increase from the birth weight. This growth trajectory is typical of small, arboreal insectivores, where a relatively extended period of dependency allows for the development of complex foraging skills necessary for locating ant and termite nests in the canopy. All developmental records discussed here were documented under controlled captive conditions maintained at 33 °C [T = 33 °C].

Reproductive output in Cyclopes didactylus is characterized by an extremely slow pace, with females producing a maximum of just 1 pup per litter [N_R_i = 1 pup per litter] and typically raising only 2 litters per year [F_R_i = 2 litters per year]. This low fecundity, observed consistently under stable captive conditions at 33 °C [T = 33 °C], positions the species among the slowest-reproducing xenarthrans. The gestation period required to bring a single pup to term lasts 135 days [tg = 135 days] at this same thermal regime of 33 °C [T = 33 °C], a duration that is relatively long for a mammal of this body size and likely reflects the metabolic constraints of a low-energy, insectivorous diet. The interval between births is therefore considerable, as the female must complete a full gestation before beginning the next reproductive cycle. This strategy of investing heavily in a single, well-developed offspring over a long gestational period is a classic K-selected life-history trait, common among small, specialized forest-dwelling mammals.

The developmental milestones of the juvenile silky anteater are tightly linked to maternal investment and occur on a protracted schedule. After parturition, the pup spends the initial phase of life clinging to the mother's back, relying entirely on her milk. The time since birth at weaning, when the juvenile transitions to solid food and becomes nutritionally independent, is 152 days [tx = 152 days] when measured under controlled conditions at 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. Following weaning, the young anteater continues to grow and develop, but it does not attain reproductive maturity quickly. For females, the time since birth at puberty, marking the onset of sexual maturity and the ability to breed, is approximately 730 days [tp = approximately 730 days] under the same thermal environment of 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. This delay of over two years between birth and the capacity to reproduce, combined with the small litter sizes, contributes to a very slow population turnover rate, making the species particularly vulnerable to habitat disturbance.

Longevity records for the silky anteater remain sparse, but captive data provide useful benchmarks. The maximum lifespan documented for this species in captivity is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years], a figure derived from observations at 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. One individual maintained under these conditions lived for 2.3 years, though this is far below the species' potential. The basal metabolic rate of Cyclopes didactylus, measured as the maximum resting oxygen consumption, averages 114.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 114.5 milliliters per hour] when the animal is at its thermoneutral zone of 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. This low metabolic rate is consistent with the species' myrmecophagous diet, which provides a relatively low caloric yield, and its generally sluggish, energy-conserving arboreal lifestyle. The metabolic and life-history data together paint a picture of an animal operating on a slow metabolic clock, with long generation times and low reproductive output.

From an ecological perspective, the life-history strategy of Cyclopes didactylus is a textbook example of adaptation to a stable, resource-poor niche. The extended gestation of 135 days [tg = 135 days] imposes a substantial energetic demand on the female, requiring her to consistently locate sufficient ant and termite colonies throughout the nursing period to support both her own maintenance and the growth of a single, slow-developing offspring at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. The weaning weight of 160 grams [Wwx = 160 grams] represents a massive maternal investment, achieved only after over five months of continuous lactation. Female adult body mass of 266 grams [Wwi = 266 grams] places this species at the smaller end of the myrmecophage body size spectrum, where the energetic constraints of a low-calorie diet are most acute.
